ts:0.prompt: You need to add a `user` property to Express's Request type across your whole codebase. Which TypeScript feature makes this possible?
options: Declaration merging: re-declaring the library's interface in a module augmentation adds the field
Intersection types: writing type Request = Request & { user: User } in a global .d.ts file
Type assertions: casting req as any wherever the user field is read inside handlers
Generic defaults: passing the user type as a type argument to express() when creating the app
ts:0.explanation: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge, which is how libraries let you augment their types (declare global / declare module 'express-serve-static-core' { interface Request { user?: User } }). Re-declaring a type alias is a 'Duplicate identifier' error, so the intersection trick doesn't work.

ts:0.prompt: What is the type of C['id']?
options: string | number
string
It's a compile error on the line that declares C
never
ts:0.explanation: An intersection requires a value to satisfy both members, so id must be string & number, which is impossible and reduces to never. Declaring C isn't an error; you only find out when you try to create a value. string | number would be the answer for a union A | B.

ts:0.prompt: Which part of this code is a compile error?
options: The type declarations, because Cat and Dog can't both declare a name property
Nothing: TypeScript lets you call any member's method on a union-typed value
p.meow(), because meow doesn't exist on Dog, so it isn't available on Cat | Dog
p.name, because a union only exposes properties that are unique to one member
ts:0.explanation: On a union you can only access members that exist on every constituent. name is shared, so p.name is fine; meow only exists on Cat, so you have to narrow first (e.g. 'meow' in p).

ts:0.prompt: Why do many teams prefer interface B extends A { ... } over type B = A & { ... } for object type hierarchies?
options: extends makes the compiled JavaScript smaller, because intersections emit helper code
extends reports conflicting property types at the declaration, while & silently produces never
extends is the only way to reuse fields; intersections copy properties at runtime
Intersections can't include methods, only data properties, so services need extends
ts:0.explanation: If B redeclares id: number while A has id: string, interface extends fails with 'incorrectly extends interface A'. The intersection compiles and quietly makes id never. The TypeScript team also notes that interfaces are cached and check faster. Neither form emits any JavaScript.

ts:0.prompt: An order service models status as type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'failed' instead of string. What's the main benefit?
options: The compiler rejects typos like 'payed' and can check switch statements for exhaustiveness
The union is converted to a runtime enum, so invalid values are rejected from the DB too
String literal unions use less memory at runtime than plain strings do in V8
It lets the status be reassigned to any string later without needing a type assertion
ts:0.explanation: Literal unions narrow the set of allowed values at compile time: typos fail, editors autocomplete, and a never check catches missing cases. They're erased at runtime, so you still need validation (e.g. zod) for data coming from a DB or HTTP.

ts:0.prompt: Which call is a compile error?
options: (2), because o has a property that Opts doesn't declare
Both, because retries isn't part of the Opts interface
Neither, because assignability in TypeScript is purely structural
(1), because excess property checks apply to fresh object literals
ts:0.explanation: Object literals passed directly are 'fresh' and get excess property checking, which catches typos like retires. Once the literal is stored in a variable, normal structural assignability applies, and extra properties are allowed.

ts:0.prompt: Does this compile under strict mode?
ts:0.code:
type U = { a: string } | { b: number };
const x: U = { a: 'x', b: 1 };
options: No: TypeScript treats object unions as exclusive, so a and b can't both be set
Yes, but only because both properties are optional in their own member types
Yes: excess property checks on a union allow any property that exists on some member
No: the literal must match exactly one member of the union, so b is an excess property
ts:0.explanation: Unions of object types aren't exclusive (XOR). The literal is assignable to { a: string }, and b exists on another member, so it isn't flagged as excess. To forbid it, add a discriminant or use { a: string; b?: never } | { b: number; a?: never }.

ts:0.prompt: Given type A = { a: string; c: number } and type B = { b: string; c: number }, what is keyof (A | B)?
options: never
ts:0.explanation: From a union you can only safely access keys present in every member, so keyof (A | B) is the common keys: 'c'. keyof (A & B) is all the keys, 'a' | 'b' | 'c'. This duality trips up a lot of people.

ts:0.prompt: Given let v: string | number, which expressions compile without narrowing? Select all that apply.
options: String(v)
v.valueOf()
v.toString()
v.toFixed(2)
v.length
ts:0.explanation: Only members common to string and number are available: toString and valueOf exist on both, and String() accepts any value. toFixed exists only on number and length only on string, so they need a typeof check first.

ts:0.prompt: Which statements about intersection types are correct? Select all that apply.
options: string & number reduces to never
A & B only keeps the properties that A and B share
They're handy for adding fields, e.g. User & { token: string }
A value of type A & B must have all the properties of both A and B
ts:0.explanation: An intersection combines requirements, so the result has every property of both types. Incompatible primitives give never. 'Only the shared properties' describes what you can access on a union, not an intersection.

ts:0.prompt: Type aliases can't be extended at all; only interfaces support reuse through extends.
options: True
False
ts:0.explanation: Type aliases are extended with intersections (type B = A & { x: number }), and an interface can extend an object-type alias (interface B extends A {}). What aliases can't do is declaration merging.

ts:1.prompt: Someone adds the 'tri' member to Shape but forgets to update area(). What happens?
options: It compiles, but TypeScript prints a warning about the unhandled 'tri' case
Runtime TypeError thrown by the never assignment the first time a triangle is passed
Compile error in the default branch: the 'tri' member isn't assignable to never
It compiles, and area() returns undefined at runtime for triangles
ts:1.explanation: In the default branch s has been narrowed to whatever cases are left. With 'tri' unhandled, that's the triangle type, which can't be assigned to never, so the build fails right where the case is missing. That's the point of the exhaustiveness check.

ts:1.prompt: Why does x.length error inside the if block?
options: The check narrows x to object, and object has no length property
typeof null is 'object', so x is narrowed to string[] | null and may still be null
typeof x === 'object' doesn't narrow at all; only instanceof narrows array types
Arrays aren't objects in TypeScript, so x is narrowed to never inside the block
ts:1.explanation: typeof narrowing follows JavaScript semantics, where typeof null === 'object'. Inside the block x is string[] | null, so strictNullChecks complains. Write if (x !== null && typeof x === 'object') or use Array.isArray(x).

ts:1.prompt: With type Fish = { swim(): void } and type Bird = { fly(): void }, what does if ('swim' in animal) do for animal: Fish | Bird?
options: Narrows animal to Fish inside the block (and to Bird in the else branch)
Nothing at compile time; the in operator only checks at runtime
Narrows animal to Fish & Bird, because both could have a swim property
Causes a compile error, because in can't be used on union types
ts:1.explanation: The in operator is a narrowing construct: the true branch keeps members that have (or may have) the property and the false branch keeps the rest. It's a handy way to tell union members apart when there's no shared discriminant field.

ts:1.prompt: What does the return type x is string give callers of isString(value) that a plain boolean return type wouldn't?
options: The compiler checks that the function body really tests for a string
The check is moved to compile time, so no runtime typeof check runs
Callers can pass only values whose static type is already string
In if (isString(v)) { ... }, v is narrowed to string inside the block
ts:1.explanation: A type predicate tells the compiler what a true result means, so the caller's variable is narrowed. TypeScript trusts you: it doesn't verify the body, so a wrong predicate leads to unsound narrowing. The function still runs at runtime as normal.

ts:1.prompt: What does an assertion function declared as function assertUser(x: unknown): asserts x is User do for the code after a call to it?
options: It narrows v only inside a following if block, like a type predicate does
It converts v to a User object by copying across the matching properties
After assertUser(v) returns, v is treated as User for the rest of the scope
It makes TypeScript generate a runtime check of User's shape automatically
ts:1.explanation: asserts x is T means 'if this function returns normally, x is T', so narrowing applies to every statement after the call. The function must throw when the check fails, and you write that check yourself; TypeScript doesn't generate validation.

options: qty is narrowed to never after the if, so the second return is unreachable
A quantity of 0 is falsy, so a valid 0 is reported as 'missing'
The ! operator doesn't narrow number | undefined, so it's a compile error
Template literals can't contain number values without calling toString()
ts:1.explanation: Truthiness narrowing removes undefined, but it also treats 0 (and NaN) as falsy. For optional numbers or strings where 0 or '' are valid, check qty === undefined (or qty == null) instead.

ts:1.prompt: Why doesn't switch (res.status) narrow res to the success or error shape?
options: status is typed string in both members, so it isn't a literal discriminant
switch statements never narrow; only if/else chains narrow unions
Discriminants have to be named kind or type for TypeScript to use them
Narrowing only works when the union has exactly two members
ts:1.explanation: A discriminated union needs a common property whose types are distinct literals, e.g. status: 'ok' and status: 'error'. With string in both members, checking the value tells the compiler nothing. switch works fine, and the property can have any name.

ts:1.prompt: In TypeScript 5.5+, what is the type of ids?
options: (number | undefined)[]
unknown[]
never[]
number[]
ts:1.explanation: TypeScript 5.5 added inferred type predicates: the arrow function x => x !== undefined is inferred as (x) => x is number, so filter returns number[]. In older versions you got (number | undefined)[] unless you wrote the predicate yourself.

ts:1.prompt: Which of these narrow a value of type string | number | Date? Select all that apply.
options: Calling a function whose return type is x is Date inside an if
Putting // @ts-ignore above the line that uses x
typeof x === 'number'
x instanceof Date
x as string
ts:1.explanation: typeof, instanceof and user-defined type predicates are narrowing constructs that affect the following code. as string is an unchecked assertion for a single expression, and @ts-ignore just hides an error; neither narrows anything.

ts:1.prompt: Which are good practices for modelling API results as a discriminated union? Select all that apply.
options: Use an in check on a property unique to one member when there's no tag
Give every member a shared, literal-typed tag field such as status: 'ok' | 'error'
Add a never-typed default branch so new members cause a compile error
Use one type where every field is optional instead of separate members
ts:1.explanation: A literal tag plus an exhaustiveness check makes impossible states unrepresentable and keeps switches complete. One all-optional type allows nonsense like both data and error being set, and forces checks everywhere. in narrowing is a valid fallback.

ts:1.prompt: With let x: string | number, writing x = 5 inside if (typeof x === 'string') { ... } is a compile error.
options: True
False
ts:1.explanation: Narrowing changes the type TypeScript tracks at each point, not the declared type. Assigning any string | number value is allowed, and after the assignment TypeScript narrows x to number for the following lines.

ts:2.prompt: What is the type of v?
options: string
string | number
unknown
'name'
ts:2.explanation: K is inferred as the literal 'name', and the return type T[K] is an indexed access type, so v is typeof u['name'], which is string. This is the classic type-safe property getter. 'name' is the type of the key, not of the value.

ts:2.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x, what does the const modifier on the type parameter change about routes?
options: The argument can't be mutated inside the function, but the type is still string[]
T must be a primitive type, so passing an array is a compile error
The function body is evaluated at compile time, like a C++ constexpr
routes is inferred as readonly ['/users', '/orders'] instead of string[]
ts:2.explanation: const type parameters (TS 5.0) make inference behave as if the caller had written as const, keeping literal and tuple types. Without it, T would be inferred as string[], and the specific route strings would be lost.

ts:2.prompt: What's the fix for the compile error 'Property length does not exist on type T'?
options: Add a default type: function longest<T = string>(a: T, b: T)
Replace the generic with any so that every property access is allowed
Constrain T: function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T)
Annotate the return type as T & { length: number } so length is known
ts:2.explanation: An unconstrained T could be anything (including number), so TypeScript won't let you read length. A constraint says which shape T must have, and the function then works for strings, arrays and any object with length while keeping the precise type. A default doesn't constrain anything.

ts:2.prompt: Given interface ApiResponse<T = unknown> { data: T; status: number }, what is the type of data in a value annotated as ApiResponse?
options: It's a compile error: generic types always need explicit type arguments
unknown
any
never
ts:2.explanation: A default type parameter is used when no argument is given, so ApiResponse means ApiResponse<unknown>. Without a default, writing ApiResponse alone would be an error ('Generic type requires 1 type argument').

ts:2.prompt: Given interface Repo<T extends { id: string }> { findById(id: string): Promise<T | null> }, what happens with let r: Repo<{ name: string }>?
options: Compile error: { name: string } doesn't satisfy the constraint { id: string }
It compiles, and findById returns Promise<{ name: string; id: string } | null>
It compiles, but r.findById is typed as returning Promise<never>
It compiles, because constraints are only checked when a method is called
ts:2.explanation: Constraints are checked wherever the generic is instantiated. { name: string } has no id, so the type argument is rejected right there ('Type does not satisfy the constraint'). TypeScript never merges the constraint into your argument.

ts:2.code:
type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type R = ToArray<string | number>;
options: (string | number)[]
never
string[] & number[]
string[] | number[]
ts:2.explanation: Conditional types distribute over unions when the checked type is a naked type parameter: ToArray<string | number> becomes ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>. To get (string | number)[] instead, turn distribution off by wrapping: [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never.

ts:2.code:
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;
type X = Unwrap<Promise<number>>;
options: unknown
never
number
Promise<number>
ts:2.explanation: infer U declares a type variable that captures whatever sits in that position when the match succeeds. Promise<number> matches Promise<infer U> with U = number. For non-promises the false branch returns T unchanged. The built-in Awaited<T> works this way and also unwraps nested promises.

ts:2.prompt: Which generic signature adds nothing over a non-generic one?
options: function wrap<T>(x: T): { value: T }
function log<T>(x: T): void, where T is used only once
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined
function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]
ts:2.explanation: A type parameter is worth having when it links two or more positions (an input to an output, or two inputs). In log it appears once, so it's equivalent to (x: unknown): void and just adds noise. The others all relate their inputs to their output types.

ts:2.prompt: Which calls compile? Select all that apply.
options: merge(1, { b: 2 })
merge([], {})
merge(null, {})
ts:2.explanation: The object type means any non-primitive, so plain objects and arrays satisfy it, but 1 (a number) doesn't. Under strictNullChecks, null isn't assignable to object, so merge(null, {}) is an error too.

ts:2.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript generics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: You can pass type arguments explicitly, as in parse<User>(raw)
Classes, interfaces and type aliases can be generic, not just functions
Generic type parameters are available at runtime through reflection by default
Type arguments are erased, so a check like x instanceof T can't work at runtime
ts:2.explanation: TypeScript erases all types when emitting JavaScript, so T has no runtime presence. If you need runtime behaviour, pass a value such as a class constructor or a zod schema. Explicit type arguments and generic classes, interfaces and aliases are all supported.

ts:2.prompt: Array<string> and string[] are the same type in TypeScript.
options: True
False
ts:2.explanation: string[] is shorthand for the generic Array<string>; the two are interchangeable. In the same way, readonly string[] is equivalent to ReadonlyArray<string>.

ts:3.prompt: Which call is a compile error?
ts:3.code:
type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string };
function update(id: string, patch: Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>) {}

update('1', { email: 'e', name: 'n' })
update('1', { id: '2' })
update('1', {})
ts:3.explanation: Omit removes id and Partial makes the rest optional, so the patch type is { name?: string; email?: string }. An empty object or any subset is fine, but id is an excess property. That's exactly the protection you want for PATCH endpoints.

ts:3.code:
type Role = 'admin' | 'user';
const perms: Record<Role, string[]> = { admin: [] };

Record<Role, ...> requires a key for every member of Role, and 'user' is missing
Record keys must be string, not a union of string literals like Role
Empty arrays can't be assigned to string[] without a type assertion
ts:3.explanation: Record<K, V> is a mapped type { [P in K]: V }, so every literal in K becomes a required property. That makes it great for exhaustive lookup tables. Use Partial<Record<Role, string[]>> if some keys are optional.

ts:3.prompt: Given function makeUser() { return { id: 1, name: 'a' }; }, how do you get its return type without writing it out?
options: ReturnType<typeof makeUser>
ReturnType<makeUser>
typeof makeUser()
ReturnType<typeof makeUser()>

ts:3.prompt: For async function fetchUser(id: string) { ... return user; } returning a User, which type gives you User?
options: ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>
Awaited<Parameters<typeof fetchUser>>
InstanceType<typeof fetchUser>
Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>
ts:3.explanation: An async function's return type is Promise<User>, so ReturnType gives Promise<User>, and Awaited unwraps it (recursively, for nested promises) to User. Parameters gives the argument tuple, and InstanceType is for constructors.

ts:3.prompt: Why is this a compile error?
ts:3.code:
type Config = { db: { host: string; port: number }; debug: boolean };
const c: Partial<Config> = { db: { host: 'x' } };

Partial makes all properties readonly, so the object literal can't be built
Partial is shallow: db is optional, but if present it still needs host and port
Partial can't be applied to types that contain nested objects
ts:3.explanation: Partial<T> only adds ? to T's top-level properties. A provided db must still be a full { host; port }. For nested patches, write a recursive DeepPartial type or use Partial on the nested type explicitly.

ts:3.prompt: A developer writes type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'pasword'> (note the typo). What happens?
options: It compiles and removes password anyway, by fuzzy-matching the key
It compiles silently, and PublicUser still includes password
Compile error: 'pasword' isn't a key of User
It compiles, but PublicUser becomes never
ts:3.explanation: Omit's key parameter is declared as K extends keyof any, so any string is accepted and omitting a nonexistent key does nothing. Pick<User, 'pasword'> would error, because Pick requires K extends keyof T. Some teams define a stricter Omit for this reason.

ts:3.prompt: What does Readonly<Config> do at runtime?
options: Nothing: it only makes the compiler reject writes to top-level properties
It calls Object.freeze on the object when it's assigned to the variable
It deep-freezes the object, including every nested property and array
It wraps the object in a Proxy that throws a TypeError on any write
ts:3.explanation: Utility types are compile-time only and are erased. Readonly is also shallow: nested objects stay mutable even at the type level. If you need runtime immutability, call Object.freeze yourself (and type it with as const or Readonly).

ts:3.prompt: Given function send(to: string, retries?: number) {}, what is Parameters<typeof send>?
options: { to: string; retries?: number }
string | number | undefined
(string | number)[]
[to: string, retries?: number]
ts:3.explanation: Parameters returns a tuple of the parameter types, keeping names as labels and optional markers. It's commonly used to write wrappers with the same arguments: (...args: Parameters<typeof send>) => send(...args).

ts:3.prompt: Which statements about built-in utility types are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Pick<T, K> requires every K to be a key of T
ReturnType<myFn> works directly on a function value named myFn
NonNullable<string | null | undefined> is string
Extract<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'a' | 'z'> is 'a'
Partial<T> makes nested object properties optional too

ts:3.prompt: Given type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string }, which types are equivalent to { name: string; email: string }? Select all that apply.

Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>
Omit<User, 'id'>
Partial<User>

ts:3.prompt: Under default strict settings, indexing a Record<string, number> with a missing key, as in counts['nope'], is typed as number rather than number | undefined unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled.

ts:4.prompt: How do you fix the compile error in this function?

Add a non-null assertion: return input!.toUpperCase();

ts:4.prompt: What's the risk in this code?

unknown
string
never

let n: never = unk;

ts:4.prompt: What's the practical difference between a function returning void and one returning never?
options: void functions can't throw errors, while never functions are required to throw

void means it returns undefined; never means it returns null
void returns normally with no useful value; never doesn't return (it throws or loops)

ts:4.prompt: What are keyof any and keyof unknown?

string | number | symbol for both
string | number | symbol, and never
never, and string | number | symbol

unknown
any

ts:4.prompt: Given let u: unknown, which of these compile? Select all that apply.

String(u)

u.foo

ts:4.prompt: Which are legitimate uses of the never type? Select all that apply.
options: The type of an optional field that may be missing
Exhaustiveness checks in the default branch of a switch
Filtering union members in conditional types, e.g. T extends X ? never : T
The return type of a function that always throws
A parameter type meaning 'accept any value'
ts:4.explanation: never represents impossibility: unreachable branches, removed union members, and functions that never return. To accept any value, use unknown. A missing optional field is undefined (or ?), not never.

ts:4.prompt: A value typed any lets you call any method on it without a compile error, and it can be assigned to a string variable without any check.

False

ts:5.prompt: This is the JavaScript tsc emits for enum Dir { Up, Down }. What does it print?

Integer-like keys come first in key order. That's why Object.keys or Object.values on a numeric enum returns twice as many entries as you might expect.

ts:5.prompt: Why do many codebases avoid const enum, especially in libraries?

const enums can't have string values, only auto-incremented numeric members
const enums are deprecated and produce a compile error in TypeScript 5.x

ts:5.prompt: A team runs .ts files directly with Node's built-in type stripping (strip-only mode, no transform). Which construct fails?

enum Color { Red, Green }

Enums (along with namespaces with runtime code and constructor parameter properties) generate JavaScript, so they need a transform. ts:5.prompt: How do you fix this so the call compiles while cfg stays an ordinary object?

Change Mode to plain string, because unions can't be used for function parameter types

ts:5.prompt: What's the advantage of satisfies here over annotating routes: Record<string, Route>?

It checks each value against Route but keeps the literal keys, so routes.typo is an error
It converts routes into a frozen object at runtime, so none of the routes can be changed later

ts:5.prompt: What happens on the last line?

ts:5.prompt: Which are real advantages of a const object plus a derived union type over a TypeScript enum? Select all that apply.
options: Plain string literals like 'admin' can be passed wherever the union type is expected
Const objects are nominally typed, so a raw string can never be passed by mistake
Enums can't be used as types in function parameters, while unions can
It's plain JavaScript, so it works with strip-only type stripping and erasableSyntaxOnly
Object.values() gives exactly the values, with no reverse-mapping entries
ts:5.explanation: The const-object pattern is erasable, iterates cleanly and accepts literals (handy for JSON input). Nominal typing is actually a property of enums, not unions, and enums can of course be used as parameter types.

ts:5.prompt: Given enum Color { Red, Green = 5, Blue }, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

Object.keys(Color).length === 3
Color.Blue === 6
Color[5] === 'Green'

ts:5.prompt: String enums get a reverse mapping at runtime, just like numeric enums.

False

ts:6.prompt: Your project sets "strict": true and you upgrade to a newer TypeScript minor version that adds a new strict-family check. What should you expect?
options: TypeScript refuses to compile until you add the new flag either on or off
The new check is enabled automatically, so the upgrade may surface new errors
Nothing changes until you list the new flag explicitly in tsconfig.json
The new check runs only as a warning until you set strict to "latest"
ts:6.explanation: strict is an umbrella that turns on the whole strict family, and the docs warn that future versions may add stricter checks under it. Upgrades can therefore break builds. To opt out of a specific check, set that individual flag to false.

options: Parameters a and b implicitly have an any type
The function's return type must be written out
a + b may be a string, so the function must be generic
Nothing, because simple functions like this one are exempt
ts:6.explanation: With no annotation and nothing to infer from, parameters would silently become any. noImplicitAny makes that an error so you annotate them (a: number, b: number). Return types are still inferred; that flag is only about implicit any.

ts:6.prompt: Under strict mode, why is this class a compile error, and which fix keeps the type honest?

Constructors can't be empty under strict mode, so add a call to super() before anything else
db isn't definitely assigned in the constructor; assign it there or inject it as a parameter

ts:6.prompt: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled, what is the type of first?

string[] | undefined
string | undefined
string

ts:6.prompt: Under strictFunctionTypes, why is f = g an error?

Parameters are checked contravariantly: g needs a Dog, but f may be called with any Animal
Function types can never be assigned to one another under strict mode
Dog is wider than Animal, so g's parameter type is incompatible the other way round

ts:6.prompt: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled and type Opts = { label?: string }, which assignment errors?

const o: Opts = {};
const o: Opts = { label: 'x' };
const o: Opts = { label: String(1) };

ts:6.prompt: A large legacy JavaScript codebase is being moved to strict TypeScript. Which approach usually works best?
options: Turn strict mode off permanently and rely on the integration tests to catch any type problems
Add // @ts-ignore above every reported error so the build passes, then turn on every flag at once
Annotate every value as any first, then remove the annotations at the end of the migration
Enable strict flags one by one (e.g. noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks), fixing errors module by module
ts:6.explanation: Turning flags on one at a time keeps the error count manageable and every step shippable. Blanket ts-ignore or any just hides the problems the migration was meant to find. Per-line @ts-expect-error with a tracking ticket is fine for leftovers, because it errors once the problem is fixed.

options: Skips type-checking your own source files and only emits the JavaScript output as fast as possible
Disables the standard lib (lib.d.ts), so globals like Promise and Map must be declared yourself
Skips type-checking all .d.ts files, which speeds up builds but can hide conflicts between library types
Stops TypeScript from resolving types from node_modules, so every import of a package becomes any

ts:6.prompt: Which compiler options are turned on by "strict": true? Select all that apply.
options: useUnknownInCatchVariables
noUncheckedIndexedAccess
exactOptionalPropertyTypes
strictNullChecks
noImplicitAny

ts:6.prompt: For a Node 22 ESM backend, which tsconfig statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: target controls which newer syntax gets down-levelled in the emitted JavaScript
lib adds runtime polyfills for the APIs it lists

ts:6.prompt: Enabling strictNullChecks doesn't add any runtime null checks to the emitted JavaScript; it only affects type checking.
options: True
False
ts:6.explanation: TypeScript's checks are erased. strictNullChecks makes null and undefined separate types the compiler tracks, but the output is the same JavaScript. Data from outside (HTTP, DB) can still be null at runtime, which is why you validate at the boundaries.

ts:7.prompt: Why is async function getCount(): number { return 1; } a compile error?

The return statement needs to be written as return await 1 in an async function
Async functions can't have return type annotations; the type is always inferred
An async function always returns a Promise, so the annotation must be Promise<number>
ts:7.explanation: Whatever an async function returns is wrapped in a Promise, so TypeScript requires the declared return type to be Promise<T> ('The return type of an async function must be the global Promise<T> type'). Returning a plain value inside is fine.

ts:7.prompt: What's wrong here, and what typically catches it?
options: save() returns Promise<void>, which can't be called from a function whose return type is string
Nothing is wrong: TypeScript reports every unawaited promise as a compile error by default
save() isn't awaited, so failures become unhandled rejections; no-floating-promises flags it
handler must be declared async or tsc refuses to compile any call to an async function from it

ts:7.prompt: Given getUser(): Promise<User> and getOrders(): Promise<Order[]>, what's the type of [u, o] in const [u, o] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getOrders()])?

ts:7.prompt: With useUnknownInCatchVariables on, what's the type-safe way to log an error message in catch (e)?

ts:7.prompt: What's the main benefit of returning type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E } instead of throwing?

TypeScript can't type thrown errors at all, so Result is the only way to type failures

ts:7.explanation: TypeScript has no checked exceptions, so a signature never tells you what it throws. A Result union makes expected failures (not found, validation) explicit, and the discriminant forces handling. Unexpected bugs still throw, so you still need error boundaries.

ts:7.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x with strict on, what's the type of err in fetchUser(id).catch((err) => { ... })?

never, because the promise is already rejected
any, because the lib types the rejection reason as any

ts:7.prompt: What is the type of users, and what's the likely bug?

ts:7.prompt: Why does 'done' print before the saves finish, and why doesn't TypeScript complain?

ts:7.prompt: Which statements about typing async code are correct? Select all that apply.

Promise<User | null> is a good return type for a lookup that may find nothing

ts:7.prompt: Which statements about typing errors in TypeScript are correct? Select all that apply.

A literal-typed code field on custom errors lets you narrow with a switch
Function signatures can't declare which errors they throw (there's no throws clause)
You can write catch (e: HttpError) to get a typed error variable

ts:7.prompt: In TypeScript, using await on a value that isn't a Promise is a compile error.

ts:8.prompt: What's the difference between schema.parse(input) and schema.safeParse(input) in zod?

parse throws a ZodError on invalid input; safeParse returns { success, data } or { success, error }
parse validates only the top-level keys; safeParse also walks into nested objects and arrays
parse returns a Promise; safeParse is the synchronous version for request handlers

ts:8.prompt: Why write type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema> instead of a separate interface User?
options: The schema becomes the single source of truth, so the runtime check and the static type can't drift apart
z.infer makes the type available at runtime, so you can check values against it with instanceof User
Interfaces can't describe optional fields or arrays, but types inferred from zod schemas can
z.infer types compile faster than handwritten interfaces, because zod caches them on disk
ts:8.explanation: With a separate interface, it's easy to change one and forget the other, leaving validation and types out of sync. Inferring the type from the schema means one definition gives you both. The inferred type is still erased at runtime; the schema is the runtime part.

ts:8.prompt: An Express handler validates req.query with z.object({ page: z.number() }) and always fails for ?page=2. Why, and what's the fix?
options: z.number() rejects values below 10; add .min(1) to the schema to allow small page numbers
req.query is a Promise in Express, so the handler has to await it before parsing
zod can't validate query strings at all; parse them by hand with parseInt() instead
Query values arrive as strings; use z.coerce.number() (with .int().min(1) as needed)

ts:8.prompt: A client sends { "name": "Ann", "isAdmin": true } to an endpoint validated by z.object({ name: z.string() }). What does parse return by default?
options: It throws, because isAdmin isn't declared in the schema
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: undefined }
{ name: 'Ann' }: unknown keys are stripped
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: true }: unknown keys pass through

ts:8.prompt: How do you validate that confirmPassword matches password and report the error on the confirmPassword field?

Add .refine((d) => d.password === d.confirmPassword, { path: ['confirmPassword'] }) to the object schema
Use z.literal(password) on the confirmPassword field, so zod compares the two values while parsing
Give both fields z.string().min(8); zod automatically compares fields that share a name prefix

ts:8.prompt: What is z.infer<typeof Schema> for Schema = z.object({ tags: z.string().transform((s) => s.split(',')) })?
options: { tags: string[] }
{ tags: string }
{ tags: string | string[] }
{ tags: unknown }
ts:8.explanation: z.infer gives the output type, after transforms. The input type (z.input<typeof Schema>) is { tags: string }. The difference matters when you type a form's values (input) versus the parsed data your service receives (output).

ts:8.prompt: Where should a Node service validate process.env with a zod schema?
options: Inside each request handler, just before the setting is read from process.env
Only in the test suite, since production environments are configured correctly
Lazily, the first time each variable is used, to keep startup as fast as possible
Once at startup, failing fast if it's invalid, then export the typed config object
ts:8.explanation: Parsing env once at boot turns a missing DATABASE_URL into an immediate, clear crash instead of a confusing failure hours later on some code path. Exporting the parsed object gives typed, coerced values (e.g. PORT as a number) everywhere.

ts:8.prompt: A mobile client sends { "nickname": null } and the schema has nickname: z.string().optional(). What happens?
options: It passes, because optional() treats null and undefined the same way
It passes, and zod coerces the null into the empty string '' for strings
Validation fails: optional() accepts undefined or a missing key, but not null
It passes, and zod converts nickname to undefined in the parsed output

ts:8.prompt: Why does PrepOS validate LLM output and request bodies with zod instead of trusting TypeScript types? Select all that apply.
options: Constraints like .max(500) also enforce size limits on untrusted text
Casting with as Answer performs a runtime check on the value
You have to write a matching interface by hand and keep it in sync with each schema
TypeScript types are erased, so nothing checks external data at runtime unless you do
parse returns data typed by the schema, turning unknown input into a trusted type
ts:8.explanation: Runtime validation is the only thing standing between untrusted input and typed code, and refinements such as lengths and enums add constraints types can't express. as is an unchecked compile-time claim, and z.infer removes the need for a separate interface.

ts:8.prompt: Which zod schemas accept the string "42" as input? Select all that apply.

z.union([z.string(), z.number()])
z.string()
z.coerce.number()
z.number()

ts:8.prompt: By default, z.object() rejects input that contains keys not declared in the schema.
options: True
False
ts:8.explanation: The default behaviour is to strip unknown keys: parsing succeeds and the extra keys are left out of the output. You have to opt in to rejecting them with z.strictObject() or .strict().
